title: 6 Best Granite Sealers in 2026: Matched to Your Slab Porosity
keywords: best sealer for porous granite countertops
description: Miracle 511 is the best granite sealer for most countertops; Tenax Hydrex for oily kitchens. 6 picks, the 5-minute water test and how to seal without haze.
dek: Miracle 511 is the best granite sealer for most countertops; Tenax Hydrex for oily kitchens.
intro: The best granite sealer for most kitchen countertops is Miracle Sealants 511 Impregnator, a proven solvent-carried sealer that repels water and oil without changing the finish. If you cook with a lot of oil or have a pale, open-grained slab, Tenax Hydrex is worth the extra money for its stronger oil resistance.

Granite varies more than most people expect. Some dark slabs are so dense that no sealer can soak in, while some light ones darken under a drop of water in under a minute. So the real job is to find out how thirsty your stone is, pick a sealer that suits it, and apply it so nothing dries on the surface. This guide covers all three, plus outdoor granite, food safety, pastes and coatings, and how often to reseal.
quickAnswer: Run a water test first: if the granite darkens within about five minutes, seal it. Miracle 511 suits most counters, Tenax Hydrex suits oily kitchens and light stone, StoneTech BulletProof is the low-odor option and Granite Gold spray is for upkeep. Apply a wet coat, let it dwell 5 to 15 minutes, then wipe off every drop and let it cure 24 to 72 hours.

sections.h: The 6 Best Granite Sealers in 2026 at a Glance

blocks.p: Every pick is an impregnator: it soaks in and lines the pores rather than forming a coating on top. That is the right kind of sealer for countertops. Film-forming acrylics and urethanes scratch, peel and make granite look plastic.
The most important step costs nothing. Drip water on the counter and watch. Plenty of dark granite never needs sealing, and the best money saved is on a product your stone cannot absorb.

sections.h: The 6 Best Granite Sealers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: These rankings draw on manufacturer data sheets, label directions, the stones each product is rated for and recurring owner feedback. Oil and water repellency, how forgiving the application is for a first-timer and how long the maker says a coat lasts on typical countertop granite carried the most weight. No product here was put through trials of our own.

Miracle 511 has been a stone-shop staple for decades because it does the core job without fuss. It soaks into medium-porosity granite and repels water and oil without changing the finish, and the maker approves it for interior and exterior use on most natural stone and on grout. The solvent carrier is thin, which helps the active ingredients travel deeper into the capillaries than many water-based products manage. The label calls for a wet coat, a few minutes of dwell time and then a complete wipe-off of the excess. On most counters one application is enough; a very thirsty slab may take a second once the first is dry. Expect a noticeable smell for an hour or two, so choose a day when you can run a fan and open windows, and turn off any gas pilot nearby. A quart normally covers an average kitchen.
**Pros:** long track record on counters, vanities and floors; no film or sheen; works on granite, marble and grout; easy to find.
**Cons:** solvent odor needs ventilation; leaves haze if excess is not wiped promptly.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Miracle+Sealants+511+Impregnator&tag=sktiger-20)

Tenax is an Italian supplier to stone fabricators, and Hydrex is its fluoropolymer impregnator for stopping both water-based and oil-based stains. Fluorinated sealers are the class that performs best against cooking oil, which ruins more light granite than anything else in a kitchen. The active ingredients are concentrated, so a small amount covers a lot of dense stone, and once cured the surface looks exactly as it did before. The routine is familiar: apply, let it soak in for the label time and buff dry. Owners commonly report water still beading years later on counters where cheaper sealers gave out within one. The trade-offs are cost and availability. It usually sells online or through stone suppliers rather than hardware stores, and a liter costs noticeably more than mainstream bottles. For a pale, open-grained slab in a kitchen that sees a lot of olive oil, that premium is easy to justify.
**Pros:** strongest oil and water repellency here; invisible on polished stone; fabricator-grade; concentrated.
**Cons:** costs more per ounce; hard to find in local stores.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Tenax+Hydrex+stain+protector&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Low-Odor Pick: StoneTech BulletProof Stone Sealer

blocks.p: BulletProof is a water-based penetrating sealer from a brand many fabricators use on their own installs. Water as the carrier means a mild smell and soap-and-water cleanup, which matters when you are sealing a kitchen the family is still using or a windowless bathroom. The maker positions it for maximum protection on porous stone and rates it for countertops, floors, showers and grout, indoors and out. On light, thirsty granite, follow the label and plan a second application after the first has soaked in. On dense dark stone, one coat is often plenty, and anything extra just sits on top waiting to haze. It leaves the surface looking untouched with no added shine. The price is high for a water-based product, but in exchange you get protection close to the solvent options without turning off the stove pilot or emptying the house for an afternoon.
**Pros:** low odor; rated for stone, tile and grout inside and out; no color or sheen change; water cleanup.
**Cons:** may need two coats on light granite; premium price for a water-based sealer.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=StoneTech+BulletProof+Stone+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Easiest Application: Granite Gold Countertop Sealer Spray

blocks.p: Granite Gold Sealer is the bottle most people find first, because it sits beside the countertop cleaners in ordinary stores. It is a water-based trigger spray: mist a clean, dry counter, let it soak briefly, then wipe and buff. That format makes it the least intimidating product here and a good way to refresh the zones that wear first, such as the strip beside the stove or the sink edge. Its limit is depth. On dense dark granite that barely absorbs anything, a light spray sealer is all you need, and it is far less likely to leave streaks than a full impregnator. On a pale, open-grained slab that darkens within a minute under a drop of water, start with a full impregnator such as Miracle 511 or BulletProof and keep this spray for upkeep. Used that way, it stretches the time between full sealings.
**Pros:** no brush or pad needed; sold almost everywhere; low odor; ideal for touch-ups.
**Cons:** lighter protection than professional impregnators; needs more frequent reapplication on porous stone.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Granite+Gold+Sealer+spray&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Outdoor Granite: StoneTech Professional Heavy Duty Sealer

blocks.p: The StoneTech Professional Heavy Duty line, long sold under the DuPont name, is a solvent-based penetrating sealer for exterior and high-traffic stone. Outdoor granite faces things an indoor counter never does: rain, sun, freeze-thaw cycles, grill grease and fallen leaves that leave tannin stains. The solvent carrier helps the active ingredients reach deep into flamed or honed granite, which is usually more porous than a polished kitchen slab. It suits outdoor kitchens, stone steps, pool coping and granite pavers. It works indoors too, but the odor is strong and a dense polished counter cannot absorb what the product is built to deliver. Wipe up all excess within the window on the label, because dried residue on polished stone takes a solvent rub to remove. Gallon sizes are available for large patios and steps.
**Pros:** built for weather and freeze-thaw; strong water and oil repellency; no change in appearance; gallon sizes.
**Cons:** strong solvent smell; more product than most indoor counters need.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=StoneTech+Heavy+Duty+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Honed Stone: Miracle Sealants Mira Enhancer

blocks.p: A color enhancer is a different tool from a plain impregnator. It seals, but it also darkens the stone and brings out the pattern, the same effect you see when granite is wet. That is welcome on honed, leathered and flamed finishes, which can look dusty or chalky, and on outdoor granite bleached by sun. It is the wrong product for a polished counter you already like, because the change is effectively permanent, and there is no easy way to pull an enhancer back out of the stone. Always try it on a hidden spot first, such as the underside of an overhang or a sink-cutout offcut, and judge it dry the next day. Apply it thinly, work in sections and remove all excess. On a leathered black or brown slab that looks gray and washed out, the result can be the difference between a slab you tolerate and one you like.
**Pros:** deepens color on honed, leathered and faded granite; seals and enhances in one step; revives weathered stone.
**Cons:** permanently darkens; not meant for highly polished surfaces; test first.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Miracle+Sealants+Mira+Enhancer&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: Does Granite Need to Be Sealed? The Water Test

blocks.p: The trade name covers dozens of stones with very different pore structures. Absolute Black and many dark gabbros are so dense a sealer has nowhere to go. Some pale whites and creams with visible crystals soak up water in under a minute.

blocks.h3: How to run the water test

blocks.p: Pour a small puddle of water on several spots, especially near the sink and cooktop, and watch.

Some stones resist water but still wick up oil. Put a few drops of vegetable oil on a hidden spot, wait 15 minutes and wipe. A dark ring that stays means a fluoropolymer sealer such as Tenax Hydrex is worth paying for.

True granite does not etch from lemon juice. If a counter sold as granite goes dull under it, the stone contains calcite and should be treated like marble; our [marble sealer guide](/best-marble-sealer/) explains how that changes the advice.

sections.h: Granite Sealers Pros and Cons: Solvent, Water-Based, Fluoropolymer and Paste

blocks.p: The thin carrier pulls active ingredients deep into tight stone, then evaporates. Pros: good penetration, proven results, fair price. Cons: odor, flammable vapors during application.

Water is the carrier, so they are nearly odorless and safer indoors. Water's higher surface tension means they may not travel as far into very dense granite, but modern products have closed most of that gap. Pros: mild smell, easy cleanup. Cons: sometimes a second coat on light stone, higher price for some brands.

Silicone and siloxane resins repel water well and oil moderately. Fluoropolymer resins repel both water and oil strongly, which is why premium products cost more. In a kitchen where olive oil and butter are daily hazards, that oil resistance is what you pay for.

Paste and cream products are usually polishes or wax-based finishes that add shine plus a light layer of repellency. They are maintenance products. They do not reach as deep as a liquid impregnator and should not be your first sealing on a porous slab.

Branded coatings such as StoneCrest's are marketed as long-term alternatives to resealing. They work differently from impregnators, so ask exactly what is applied, how scratches are repaired and what the written warranty covers before paying.

sections.h: What Is the Best Sealer for Porous, Dark or Honed Granite?

blocks.p: Absolute Black, Uba Tuba, Black Pearl and similar stones rarely need more than a light maintenance spray, and often nothing at all. Over-applying here is the most common cause of hazy streaks. If water barely darkens the stone, a yearly pass with Granite Gold is the most you should do.

The big middle group of browns, golds and speckled patterns is where a standard impregnator such as Miracle 511 or StoneTech BulletProof earns its keep. One full coat after installation, then a reseal every one to three years guided by the water test.

Many whites, creams and stones with large crystals or visible fissures absorb a lot and show oil rings and coffee stains. Use a premium oil-repelling sealer like Tenax Hydrex, apply two coats and test again after a week. Some of these slabs are resin-treated at the factory, which helps, but resin does not fill every pore.

These are always more absorbent than the polished version of the same stone because the finishing process opens the surface. Seal them more generously and consider an enhancer like Mira Enhancer if the finish looks washed out.

Seam filler is epoxy or polyester and needs no sealer, but the stone edges on either side were cut on site and often absorb more than the field. Give the inch beside each seam, the sink rim and the cooktop cutout an extra pass.

sections.h: How Do You Seal Granite Countertops Without Leaving Haze?

blocks.p: Clean with a pH-neutral stone cleaner, never vinegar or bleach, and lift any stains first, because sealer locks in whatever is already in the pores. Let the counter dry at least 24 hours, longer around the sink.

Work about 3 by 3 feet at a time. Use a lint-free cloth, foam brush or the spray nozzle so the surface looks evenly wet. Let it dwell for the label time, usually 5 to 15 minutes, and keep it wet by adding product where it soaks in fast.

blocks.h3: Wipe off every bit of excess

blocks.p: This step decides how the job looks. Wipe with clean, dry cloths and buff until the counter feels like bare stone with no tackiness. Change cloths as they get damp. If a second coat is needed, wait the label interval, typically 20 minutes to a few hours.

Most impregnators reach handling strength in a few hours but need 24 to 72 hours to fully cure. Keep water, oil and acidic food off it and do not judge the result with a water test until the cure window has passed. If haze shows the next day, rub it with a little of the same sealer on a cloth and buff dry.

A dense dark granite may take a quart over 300 to 600 square feet, a thirsty light one over 100 to 200. A typical kitchen has 30 to 60 square feet of counter, so one quart covers two coats with room to spare. Outdoor kitchens and stone steps are where gallon sizes make sense.

sections.h: How Often Should You Seal Granite, and Should You Hire a Pro?

blocks.h3: Let the water test set the schedule

blocks.p: There is no fixed interval. Test once a year near the sink and stove. When water darkens the stone within about five minutes, reseal. Dense counters often go three to five years or longer; porous slabs may need sealing every year.

Cleaning, mostly. Vinegar, lemon sprays, bleach, ammonia and many bathroom cleaners are acidic or strongly alkaline and break impregnators down. Daily, use a neutral stone cleaner or a few drops of dish soap in warm water.

A dark ring that fades within an hour or two is water evaporating out of the stone, a sign the seal near that spot is thinning. A light, dull ring is hard-water mineral that wipes off with a neutral cleaner and a soft pad.

For oil, a poultice of absorbent powder and acetone, covered with plastic for 24 to 48 hours, usually pulls it out. For coffee or wine on light stone, a hydrogen peroxide poultice often works; test on a hidden spot first. Reseal afterward, since poultices draw out sealer too.

Stone-care companies commonly quote about $150 to $300 or more for a sealing visit. That makes sense when the counter also needs polishing, chip repair or deep stain removal. For a routine reseal, a quart of good impregnator and an hour of your time gives the same result, because the chemistry is the same.

sections.h: How Do You Seal Outdoor Granite?

blocks.p: Outdoor kitchens, pool coping and stair treads face sun, rain, freeze-thaw cycles, sprinklers and leaf and berry stains. Most exterior granite has a flamed finish for grip, which is rougher and more porous than a polished slab.

Choose an impregnator rated for exterior use, such as StoneTech Professional Heavy Duty. Breathability matters outside: moisture that gets into stone from below or the edges must escape as vapor. A film traps it and can cause spalling or white deposits in cold climates. The same principle drives our advice on [exterior brick sealers](/best-brick-sealer-reviews/).

Clean with a stone-safe cleaner and a low-pressure rinse rather than a high-pressure blast, which can etch soft mineral veins. Allow 48 hours of dry weather, apply between about 50 and 90 degrees Fahrenheit and avoid direct midday sun, which can flash the carrier off before the sealer soaks in.
Granite pavers set in sand behave like any paver system; our [paver sealer guide](/best-paver-sealer/) covers joint sand and edges. Expect to reseal outdoor granite every one to three years.

Once cured, reputable impregnating sealers are generally considered fine for food-prep counters. The active ingredients sit inside the stone and the carrier evaporates completely. Several makers say so on their data sheets; check the label or safety data sheet for your product if it matters to you.

Solvent products release VOCs and flammable vapors. Turn off pilot lights, do not run gas burners nearby, ventilate well and keep children and pets out until the smell is gone. Water-based products are much milder but still need their full cure time.

Wait the full cure period, typically 24 to 72 hours, before putting food directly on the counter. After that, wash the surface once with a neutral stone cleaner. If anyone at home is sensitive to fumes, choose StoneTech BulletProof or Granite Gold and seal on a day the windows can stay open.

mistakes: Sealing granite that cannot absorb anything

Dense stones such as Absolute Black will not take sealer, and applying it anyway leaves a sticky, streaky film that needs solvent to remove. Do the water test first; if the stone stays unchanged after half an hour, skip the sealer.
Letting excess sealer dry on top

An impregnator only works inside the stone. Anything left on the surface after the dwell time cures into haze that shows in raking light. Buff with clean, dry cloths until the counter feels like bare stone, and swap cloths as soon as they get damp.

Sealer locks in whatever is already in the pores. Poultice out oil rings or coffee spots first and let the stone dry for a day or two. Sealing over a stain makes it permanent and keeps a poultice from working later.

Acidic and harsh alkaline cleaners break down impregnators and shorten the seal dramatically. They can also dull slabs that contain some calcite, which many stones sold as granite do. Switch to a pH-neutral stone cleaner or mild dish soap.
Using a concrete or garage-floor coating on a counter

Acrylic and urethane coatings made for driveways form a film that scratches, yellows and peels on a countertop, and they make the stone look plastic. They are also miserable to strip. Use only impregnating sealers rated for natural stone where food is prepared.
bottomLine: For most kitchen granite, Miracle Sealants 511 Impregnator is the safe, proven choice. If you cook with a lot of oil or have a light, open-grained slab, spend more on Tenax Hydrex; if solvent fumes are a problem, StoneTech BulletProof gives nearly the same protection with water-based convenience; and for outdoor stone, use an exterior-rated product such as StoneTech Professional Heavy Duty. Run the water test before you buy anything, because plenty of dark granite needs no sealer at all, and when you do seal, wipe off every drop of excess.

faqs.q: What is the best granite sealer for countertops?
faqs.a: Miracle Sealants 511 Impregnator is the best granite sealer for most countertops: proven, widely sold and invisible once wiped off. For kitchens with heavy oil use or pale, porous slabs, Tenax Hydrex gives stronger oil resistance. If solvent odor is a problem, StoneTech BulletProof offers similar protection in a water-based formula.

faqs.q: How often should granite countertops be sealed?
faqs.a: There is no fixed schedule. Do a water test once a year; if a puddle darkens the stone within about five minutes, reseal. Dense dark granite may go five years or more, or never need it, while light, porous slabs can need sealing every year. Test near the sink and stove first.

faqs.q: What is the best sealer for porous granite countertops?
faqs.a: A fluoropolymer impregnator such as Tenax Hydrex, applied in two coats, is the best choice for porous granite because it resists both water and oil. Let the first coat soak in, apply the second within the label window, wipe off all excess and recheck with a water test after a week.

faqs.q: Is sealing granite countertops a DIY job?
faqs.a: Yes. Sealing granite is one of the easiest stone-care jobs. You need a clean, dry counter, the sealer and a stack of lint-free cloths. Apply, wait the dwell time on the label and buff off all excess. It usually takes under an hour plus cure time and costs far less than a professional visit.

faqs.q: Will granite sealer change the color of my countertop?
faqs.a: A standard impregnating sealer should not change color or sheen once the excess is wiped off. Color-enhancing sealers are the exception: they darken the stone on purpose and the effect is largely permanent. If a regular sealer leaves the counter cloudy, that is surface residue, which a little fresh sealer on a cloth removes.

faqs.q: Is granite sealer paste better than liquid sealer?
faqs.a: Not for the main sealing. Paste and cream products are usually polishes or wax-based finishes that add shine and light repellency, which suits upkeep on a counter that is already sealed. A liquid impregnator penetrates deeper and lasts longer, so use one for the first sealing on any slab that fails the water test.

faqs.q: How long after sealing granite can I use the counter?
faqs.a: Most impregnators allow light use within a few hours, but full cure usually takes 24 to 72 hours. During that time keep water, oil and acidic foods off the surface and do not set anything wet on it. Check the label for its cure window and wait until it passes before judging the result.
